title: Self-Storage Replacement Sourcing
name: Self-Storage Replacement Sourcing
metaTitle: Self-Storage Replacement Sourcing in Denver, CO
metaDescription: Sourcing self-storage facilities for 1031 exchange investors trading out of apartments or retail across metro Denver's growth corridors.

sections.html: A fair number of the self-storage inquiries we get come from apartment owners tired of tenant turnover and 2 a.m. maintenance calls. Storage facilities take less day-to-day management, and metro Denver's growth corridors keep generating renters who need somewhere to put belongings during a move. That combination makes storage a common landing spot for exchange dollars leaving a management-heavy asset class.

sections.heading: Why storage demand tracks in-migration
sections.html: Front Range in-migration means a steady stream of people moving into and around metro Denver, downsizing between apartments, or waiting on a home purchase to close. All of that creates storage demand that doesn't depend much on broader retail or office conditions. Facilities near dense apartment corridors in Aurora and along I-70 tend to run higher occupancy than ones stuck in low-density areas without nearby renter demand.

sections.heading: What separates a strong facility from a weak one
sections.html: Climate-controlled unit mix matters more each year, since renters increasingly expect it and older drive-up-only facilities without climate control lose out on pricing power. We also look at unit size distribution; a facility overloaded with large units competes for a smaller pool of renters than one with a good spread of small and mid-size units, which turn over more often and at higher effective rent per square foot.

sections.heading: Operational handoff after closing
sections.html: Most self-storage facilities sell with a third-party management company already in place or an easy transition to one, which is a big part of the appeal for an investor leaving a hands-on asset class. We confirm the management contract terms and fee structure before a facility goes on the identification list, since a below-market management fee sometimes signals an operator who's underinvesting in the facility's marketing and upkeep.

sections.heading: Facility types we track
sections.html:
The self-storage stock across metro Denver's growth corridors generally splits into a few categories:

  • Climate-controlled interior-access facilities in denser suburban corridors
  • Drive-up exterior-access facilities along I-70 and outer suburban roads
  • Mixed facilities combining both unit types under one roof or campus
  • Facilities with attached RV, boat, or vehicle storage yards
  • Newer construction facilities still in initial lease-up

sections.heading: Watchouts before we recommend a facility
sections.html: A facility still in lease-up needs the same caution as a new apartment building, since a pro forma occupancy number means nothing until renters actually show up. We also check for nearby competing facilities under construction, since a saturated corridor can flatten rate growth for years even if current occupancy looks strong today.

sections.heading: How management structure affects the numbers
sections.html: A facility run by a national third-party operator typically carries higher, more consistent rate management through automated pricing tools that adjust street rates by unit type and demand, which usually shows up as steadier revenue on the T12. A facility run independently by the owner can still perform well, but the numbers depend more heavily on that owner's discipline around raising existing-tenant rates over time, something we check by comparing new-tenant rates against existing-tenant rates on the rent roll.

sections.heading: Why exchange timing works in storage's favor
sections.html:
Self-storage transactions tend to move at a more predictable pace than a competitive multifamily bidding situation in RiNo or LoDo, since the buyer pool is smaller and more specialized. That gives an exchange investor a bit more breathing room inside the 45-day identification window, though we still recommend having a backup candidate ready in case financing terms shift or a seller receives a stronger competing offer late in the process.

We also keep a short list of facilities that weren't quite ready to sell when an investor's exchange began, since storage owners often test the market informally before listing, and knowing which facilities might come available inside the identification window can turn a thin pipeline into a workable one.

We keep those informal conversations going year-round rather than starting them cold once an investor's 45-day window has already begun, since a storage owner deciding whether to sell often takes months to make that decision regardless of how ready a buyer is.

That patience has paid off more than once, turning a quiet conversation from a year earlier into a real closing once an investor's exchange timeline finally lined up with an owner who was, at last, genuinely ready to move on and retire from the business.

faqs.q: Why are apartment owners moving exchange dollars into self-storage?
faqs.a: Storage facilities generally require far less day-to-day management than an apartment building, with fewer tenant issues and lower turnover cost per unit, which appeals to owners looking to step back from active landlord duties.

faqs.q: Does climate-controlled storage really rent better than drive-up storage?
faqs.a: In most Denver submarkets, yes. Renters increasingly expect climate control, and facilities without it often have to discount rates to stay competitive against newer climate-controlled product nearby.

faqs.q: How do you evaluate a self-storage facility that's still filling up after opening?
faqs.a: We look at month-over-month absorption pace rather than the operator's stabilized pro forma, since a newly opened facility hasn't proven it can hit projected occupancy yet.

faqs.q: Does a self-storage facility come with a management company already in place?
faqs.a: Often, yes, either through a franchise-style third-party operator or an easy transition to one. We review the existing management contract's fee structure and terms before recommending a facility.

faqs.q: What's the biggest risk with buying a self-storage facility right now?
faqs.a: New supply. A corridor with several facilities under construction nearby can flatten rate growth for years, even if the facility you're buying currently shows strong occupancy.
